messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Imani was a woman who had built her life, and her career as an architect, on the principles of stability and foresight. For forty-seven years, she had believed in controllable risks and predictable outcomes. That belief shattered nine months ago, on a bright, windswept Tuesday at a downtown construction site. She was reviewing the installation of a complex steel truss when she gave the go-ahead to remove a temporary shoring brace. The sequence was standard, but something was wrong. A low groan of stressed metal, a sound she now hears in her sleep, was followed by a sharp crack and a partial collapse. A young foreman fell two stories, sustaining life-altering injuries. In the chaotic aftermath, the air thick with dust, Imani tasted grit and a coppery tang of fear that still coats her tongue whenever the memory returns.

In the first few weeks, she tried to force a coherent narrative of the event, to map it out like a blueprint, but found she couldn't deliberately access the memory in a linear way (Hard to Recall Deliberately). Instead, it ambushed her in fragments. The sickening screech of the steel (Auditory Recall) would slice through a quiet meeting, or the metallic taste of dust (Taste Vividness) would rise in her throat while she was drinking her morning coffee. These sensory intrusions were terrifyingly real, and each time one broke through, her body reacted as if the danger were present (Memory → Threat). A car backfiring would send a jolt of panic through her, leaving her heart hammering against her ribs (Startle to Sounds, False Alarms). The memory also brought an immediate, crushing wave of self-recrimination; she saw not just the accident, but her own failure, her own unique inadequacy that allowed it to happen (Memory → Negative Appraisals). Overwhelmed by these intrusive flashbacks, she found herself replaying the moments leading up to the collapse for hours, endlessly searching for the fatal error she was certain she had made (Memory → Maladaptive Strategies).

This internal state of high alert began to corrode her sense of self. The constant, thrumming anxiety made it impossible to focus at work, her mind skittering away from the complex calculations her job required (Concentration). This persistent feeling of being on edge only reinforced her belief that she was fundamentally broken, no longer the competent professional she had once been (Threat → Negative Appraisals). When the sudden slam of a door in her office made her flinch violently, the ensuing rush of adrenaline would trigger a desperate need to regain control. She would immediately start counting the acoustic tiles on the ceiling, grouping them into sevens, a silent, frantic ritual she believed could somehow prevent another disaster from unfolding (Threat → Maladaptive Strategies). The state of hypervigilance also made her more susceptible to the past; being startled primed her mind to snag on any reminder, pulling the fragmented memory of the collapse back to the surface (Threat → Memory).

Her days are now governed by a punishing internal logic. The conviction that she is irrevocably changed and set apart from her colleagues—who she imagines must see her as a liability—has become the bedrock of her experience (Isolation, Unrecognisable Self). This deep sense of personal failure fuels her maladaptive coping strategies (Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies). She spends hours dwelling on what she has done wrong (Self-Blame Rumination), a form of self-punishment that offers no resolution. To escape the sheer horror, she will sometimes tell herself that at least the foreman is alive, that it could have been worse (Downward Comparison), but the relief is fleeting. This constant rumination, this forced re-engagement with her perceived mistakes, ensures the traumatic memory remains fresh and accessible, ready to intrude at the slightest provocation (Maladaptive Strategies → Memory). The rituals and the rumination do not soothe her; instead, they keep the event "live" in her mind, feeding her anxiety and leaving her perpetually braced for another catastrophe (Maladaptive Strategies → Threat). This cycle of self-blame has become a cage, reinforcing the very beliefs that drive it; the more she ruminates, the more she feels like a contemptible person, utterly alone in her guilt (Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals). Her belief that a better architect would have prevented the accident colours the memory itself, making it almost impossible to recall any detail that doesn't confirm her culpability (Negative Appraisals → Memory).

Imani finally sought therapy last week. Her firm had assigned her a new high-rise project, and the thought of bearing that level of structural responsibility again filled her with a dread so profound it was paralyzing. She has not been to a construction site in months, sending junior colleagues in her place. Her husband says he no longer recognizes the vibrant, confident woman he married. Imani agrees. She feels like a ghost in her own life, haunted by the sound of breaking steel and the unshakable belief that she is a dangerous person who doesn't deserve to build things anymore.
